sections.normalized_html: When a sine wave is shifted horizontally from its usual position, we say that the function has undergone a phase shift.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x,] graphed below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3ebf2e82beec5a617c33f9d8c0ced560]

Content:
We can move the graph right (or left) by subtracting (or adding) a number from [MATH: x] inside the sine function. These are horizontal translations.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's plot the graph of [MATH: y=\sin \left( x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).] To do this, we shift the sine function [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2}] units to the right.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4eaef0ed73d8420efa0fbbd5f468c5c3]

Content:
This might seem counterintuitive: subtracting a number from [MATH: x] inside the sine function shifts the graph to the right, in the positive direction of the [MATH: x]-axis. But this is in fact true.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the point [MATH: x=\pi.] By substituting it into our function, we get
[MATH: y|= \sin (x − (π)/(2)); = \sin (π − (π)/(2)); = \sin ((π)/(2)); = 1.]
So, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right)] on the graph is now [MATH: \left(\pi,1\right)] and we obtain a shift to the right.

Content:
Similarly, we plot the graph of [MATH: y=\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)] by shifting the sine function [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{3}] units to the left.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ee21d1733ae0ec5a645d055007d35f3e]

Content:
When a sine wave is shifted horizontally from its usual position, we say that the function has undergone a phase shift.

items.title: Finding a Vertical Asymptote for a Horizontally Translated Tangent Function

sections.normalized_html: The graph below shows one branch of the curve [MATH: y=\tan(x+C)] for some number [MATH: C,] where [MATH: -\dfrac\pi 2 < C < \dfrac \pi 2,] and a vertical asymptote of the curve. What is the equation of the vertical asymptote?
sections.readable_text:
The graph below shows one branch of the curve [MATH: y=\tan(x+C)] for some number [MATH: C,] where [MATH: -\dfrac\pi 2 < C < \dfrac \pi 2,] and a vertical asymptote of the curve. What is the equation of the vertical asymptote?

[IMG: /graphics/be7bd3276dc8a4b0640619dd6d67150e]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's add the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x] to the plot.

To plot the given curve, we follow these steps:

  • Start with the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x.]

  • Then, shift it by [MATH: \dfrac 12] units left.

Therefore, the given graph is [MATH: y = \tan\left(x+\dfrac 1 2\right),] which means [MATH: C=\dfrac 1 2.]

Since the graph is shifted by [MATH: \dfrac 12] units left, the asymptote is also shifted by [MATH: \dfrac 12] units left.

The corresponding asymptote on the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x] is [MATH: x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}.] Therefore, the equation of the asymptote shown is

[MATH: x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac 12 = -\dfrac{\pi+1}{2}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's consider the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x,] graphed below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3ebf2e82beec5a617c33f9d8c0ced560]

Content:
We can move the graph right (or left) by subtracting (or adding) a number from [MATH: x] inside the sine function. These are horizontal translations.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's plot the graph of [MATH: y=\sin \left( x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).] To do this, we shift the sine function [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2}] units to the right.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4eaef0ed73d8420efa0fbbd5f468c5c3]

Content:
This might seem counterintuitive: subtracting a number from [MATH: x] inside the sine function shifts the graph to the right, in the positive direction of the [MATH: x]-axis. But this is in fact true.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the point [MATH: x=\pi.] By substituting it into our function, we get
[MATH: y|= \sin (x − (π)/(2)); = \sin (π − (π)/(2)); = \sin ((π)/(2)); = 1.]
So, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right)] on the graph is now [MATH: \left(\pi,1\right)] and we obtain a shift to the right.

Content:
Similarly, we plot the graph of [MATH: y=\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)] by shifting the sine function [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{3}] units to the left.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ee21d1733ae0ec5a645d055007d35f3e]

Content:
When a sine wave is shifted horizontally from its usual position, we say that the function has undergone a phase shift.

---

To plot the given curve, we follow these steps:

- Start with the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.]
- Then, shift it by [MATH: 1] unit right.

Therefore, the given graph is [MATH: y = \sin\left(x-1\right).]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Horizontally Translating the Tangent Function

Content:

Content:
To obtain the graph of [MATH: y=\tan \left( x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right),] we translate the tangent function by [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{4}] units to the right, as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/abf51bf53ed88e2fc187aaee64823468]

Content:
Note that the asymptotes of [MATH: y=\tan\left( x-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)] are also shifted to the right by [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{4}.] For example, the first asymptote to the right of the [MATH: y]-axis is now
[MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+ \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.]

Content:
Similarly, to obtain the graph of [MATH: y=\tan \left( x+1\right),] we translate the tangent function by [MATH: 1] unit to the left, as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3065aef745350f81365002fc05fb8eea]

Content:
Note that the asymptotes of [MATH: y=\tan\left( x+1 \right)] are also shifted to the left by [MATH: 1.] For example, the first asymptote to the right of the [MATH: y]-axis is now
[MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-1.]

Item 13 — Example: Finding a Vertical Asymptote for a Horizontally Translated Tangent Function

Example Prompt:
The graph below shows one branch of the curve [MATH: y=\tan(x+C)] for some number [MATH: C,] where [MATH: -\dfrac\pi 2 < C < \dfrac \pi 2,] and a vertical asymptote of the curve. What is the equation of the vertical asymptote?

[IMG: /graphics/be7bd3276dc8a4b0640619dd6d67150e]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's add the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x] to the plot.

[IMG: /graphics/ee98ef0113a80965b7e45b717a595d11]

To plot the given curve, we follow these steps:

- Start with the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x.]
- Then, shift it by [MATH: \dfrac 12] units left.

Therefore, the given graph is [MATH: y = \tan\left(x+\dfrac 1 2\right),] which means [MATH: C=\dfrac 1 2.]

Since the graph is shifted by [MATH: \dfrac 12] units left, the asymptote is also shifted by [MATH: \dfrac 12] units left.

The corresponding asymptote on the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x] is [MATH: x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}.] Therefore, the equation of the asymptote shown is

[MATH: x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac 12 = -\dfrac{\pi+1}{2}.]
